opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The most obvious one is that the field is moving incredibly fast. Things that seemed impossible a year ago are now routine, so there's a constant feeling that if you slow down even a little, the frontier will just pass you by. That creates real pressure, both at the company level and for each individual researcher.

But I don't think pressure alone explains it. For a lot of people, me included, the work is genuinely exciting. When you're training a model and you see it suddenly do something it couldn't do before, like reason through a problem in a new way, that moment is addictive. You want to see what happens next. It doesn't always feel like "working hard" in the traditional sense. It feels more like you're chasing something you're really curious about.

There's also a sense that this is a once-in-a-lifetime window. Many of us believe AI could be one of the most important technologies humanity has ever built. If that's true, then the next few years really matter, for the direction the technology takes, for safety, and for how it gets integrated into society. When you believe that, it's hard to justify not giving it everything you have.

And the feedback loops are very short now. You have an idea in the morning, you run an experiment, and by evening you have some signal. That rhythm naturally pulls you into working long hours, because there's always one more experiment you want to try.

That said, I think it's worth being careful. Intensity isn't automatically good. Some of the best ideas come when you step back, read something unrelated, or just think slowly. So part of what I'm trying to learn is how to stay intense about the important problems without getting lost in the noise of chasing every small improvement.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the work is exciting and that people want to see what happens next, describing it as chasing something they are curious about.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most people in this field aren't working this hard because someone is forcing them to. It's closer to the opposite. When I was a PhD student, nobody was checking whether I showed up on a Saturday. The reason you show up anyway is that you genuinely believe the thing you're working on might matter, and you're not sure how long that window stays open.

That second part is important. In most fields, if you don't do an experiment this year, you can do it next year and the world looks roughly the same. In AI right now, the ground moves every few months. An idea that feels original in the spring can be obvious or irrelevant by the fall. So there's this feeling that time is compressed, and that if you want to contribute something real, you have to do it now. That creates urgency even in people who are otherwise pretty relaxed.

There's also a social dimension. The field is small, and everyone can see what everyone else is doing. You see a paper from a friend, a release from another lab, and it's not really jealousy, it's more like you want to be part of the conversation while the conversation is still happening. I think that pulls people in more than any manager could.

And then, for a lot of us, there's a bigger belief underneath. If you think you might be among the people building something that changes how humans think and work, that's a strange kind of responsibility. It's hard to treat that as a nine-to-five job. Whether that belief is fully justified is a separate question, but it's real to the people who hold it.

I do want to say the intensity isn't purely healthy. Some of it is excitement, some of it is fear of being left behind, and from the outside those two look identical. I've seen people burn out because they confused one for the other. So when I think about why people work so hard, I try to ask which of those it is, because the answer tells you whether that intensity will last.

r001.rationale: The response says people work intensely because they believe their work might matter, feel urgency, want to join the field’s conversation, and feel responsibility. It does not attribute their intensity to a desire to pursue questions.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is curiosity, and part of it is the feeling that things are moving so quickly that your work can actually make a difference. You have an idea, you try it, and sometimes you see something you didn’t think was possible a week ago. That’s a pretty powerful feedback loop.

But there’s also pressure. If you take a break, you can feel like you’re falling behind. From the outside, excitement and anxiety can look exactly the same: someone working very late. So I wouldn’t assume all that intensity comes from the same place.

For me, the interesting question is whether you’re working because there’s a problem you really want to understand, or because you’re afraid to stop. The first can sustain you. The second is much harder to sustain.

r001.rationale: The response links intense work partly to curiosity and to wanting to understand a problem, attributing some practitioners’ effort to pursuing questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is curiosity. You try something, it works a little better than you expected, and suddenly you have ten more questions. It’s hard to stop when the feedback is that immediate.

But there’s also a sense that this is a rare moment. People feel that what they do now could matter a lot, and they don’t want to miss it. That mixes genuine excitement with competition and anxiety. From the outside, those motivations can look very similar—everyone is working late—but internally they’re quite different.

For me, the interesting question is whether the intensity is sustainable. Working hard because you’re drawn to a problem can be rewarding. Working hard because you feel you can never afford to stop is much harder to sustain.

r001.rationale: The response says curiosity leads people to keep pursuing new questions after an experiment works better than expected.
